title: The Benko Gambit
subtitle: A pawn for permanent pressure on the queenside
summary: Black offers a queenside pawn, sometimes two, in exchange for open a- and b-files, a monster fianchettoed bishop, and pressure that can last the entire game -- even into an endgame, unlike most gambits.

rootAnnotations.title: A positional gambit, not a tactical one
rootAnnotations.body: Unlike the King's Gambit, Black is not trying to attack the king quickly. The Benko trades a queenside pawn for lasting structural assets: open files for the rooks and a powerful bishop on the long diagonal. This compensation does not evaporate -- it is just as real in a simplified endgame as in the middlegame, which is unusual for a gambit and is exactly why it has been trusted at every level, including the World Championship.

annotations.title: The gambit pawn
annotations.body: Black offers a queenside pawn at once. The point is not to win it back quickly -- it's to blast open the a- and b-files and develop the light-squared bishop with tempo before White can consolidate the extra material.

annotations.title: Re-offering material
annotations.body: Black is often willing to give up a second pawn here rather than recapture immediately with a piece. Opening the a-file before White finishes developing is worth more than the pawn.

annotations.title: Developing with a threat
annotations.body: Recapturing with the bishop, not a future ...Nxa6 or the c8-pawn structure, is the whole point: the bishop lands on a6 already eyeing f1 along the long light diagonal and the rook on a8 is already staring down the open a-file.
Black solidifies the center before finishing development, keeping options open for ...e6, ...Nbd7, or ...Qa5 depending on how White sets up.

annotations.title: Preparing the real point of the opening
annotations.body: g6 sets up the fianchetto that gives the Benko its long-term power: a dark-squared bishop bearing down the entire a1-h8 diagonal.
White mirrors the fianchetto, aiming to neutralize the long diagonal and finish development safely -- the main modern try against the Benko.

annotations.title: The engine of Black's compensation
annotations.body: This bishop is the single most important piece in the Benko. From g7 it presses b2 and d4 for the entire game and supports tactics like ...Nb4 or a future exchange sacrifice on a1 or c3, all built on the pressure already generated on the queenside.

annotations.title: Compensation that outlasts the middlegame
annotations.body: Black is down a pawn but both rooks are already aimed at White's queenside without having moved, the bishop pair is gone but the surviving g7-bishop is excellent, and simple plans like ...Qa5, ...Rfb8, and doubling on the a-file give lasting pressure. This is why the Benko is famous for holding up even when the game is simplified into an endgame.
